blocks.text: "The shop was burgled last night." Nobody in that sentence is accused of anything, and yet the whole event is reported. Newspapers, police statements, laboratory reports and government circulars all lean on the passive voice for exactly that reason — it lets you describe an action without naming who performed it.

blocks.title: Voice
blocks.text: The form of a verb that shows whether the subject performs the action or receives it. In the active voice the subject acts. In the passive voice the subject is acted upon, and the verb becomes a form of *be* plus a past participle.

blocks.markdown:
### Turning active into passive: four moves

1. Move the **object** of the active sentence into the subject position.
2. Insert the correct form of **be**, keeping the original tense.
3. Change the main verb to its **past participle**.
4. Put the original subject after **by** — or drop it if it adds nothing.

**Active:** The council repaired the road.
**Passive:** The road **was repaired** by the council.

Only **transitive** verbs can be made passive, because a verb with no object has nothing to promote to subject.

blocks.caption: The passive keeps the tense of the active sentence unchanged

blocks.title: Making a two-object sentence passive
blocks.prompt: Change to the passive voice, keeping the person as the subject: "The school awarded Amina a scholarship."

steps.text: Find both objects. *Amina* is the indirect object — she receives the benefit. *A scholarship* is the direct object — it is the thing given.
Decide which one the question wants at the front. It asks for the person, so *Amina* becomes the subject.
Identify the tense of the active verb. *Awarded* is simple past, so the form of *be* must also be simple past: *was*.
Add the past participle: *awarded*. This gives 'Amina was awarded ...'.
Leave the remaining object in place: 'Amina was awarded a scholarship'.
Add the agent after *by*: 'Amina was awarded a scholarship by the school.' Note that the other version, 'A scholarship was awarded to Amina by the school', is also grammatical.

blocks.answer: Amina was awarded a scholarship by the school.

items: Use the **active** voice by default: it is shorter, clearer and states responsibility.
Use the **passive** when the doer is unknown: *The shop was burgled last night.*
Use the **passive** when the doer is obvious or irrelevant: *The suspect was arrested on Sunday.*
Use the **passive** in scientific and technical reports, where the procedure matters more than the person: *The mixture was heated for ten minutes.*
Use the **passive** when you want the receiver to be the focus of the sentence: *Amina was awarded the scholarship.*

blocks.title: Keep the tense; do not add *been* after a modal
blocks.text: Two errors dominate this topic. First, shifting tense during the change — *has approved* must become *has been approved*, not *was approved*. Second, writing *must been submitted*; after a modal the correct form is *must be submitted*.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: In a transformation question, write the be-form first and the participle second before you assemble the sentence. Deciding the tense of *be* on its own prevents the commonest slip, which is producing a grammatical sentence in the wrong tense.

points: In the active voice the subject acts; in the passive voice the subject is acted upon.
The passive is always a form of *be* plus a past participle.
Only transitive verbs can be made passive, because the object becomes the new subject.
The tense of the original sentence must be preserved in the transformation.
After a modal, use *be* plus the participle, never *been*.
Prefer the active voice unless the doer is unknown, unimportant or best left unnamed.
